parts: Lesson 22: Consumer! Beware, Be Aware — Summary
Who is a consumer; problems faced

A consumer is a person who buys or uses goods or services to satisfy needs. The Consumer Protection Act (CPA) 1986 recognises one who buys and uses goods and one who hires or avails a service for personal use. Problems of consumers: (1) Price variation – the Maximum Retail Price (MRP) printed on the product includes all taxes; never pay more, and take a receipt; (2) lack of standardised products – substandard goods give shopkeepers higher commission; compare brands on price, standard mark, ease of use, after-sales service, electricity use and warranty; (3) imitation – look-alike packs and names (Colgate and 'college') and fake standard marks, a punishable offence; (4) adulteration – adding inferior substances or removing a vital part to earn more profit; (5) non-availability, black-marketing and hoarding; (6) defective weights and measures; (7) misleading or no information – tiny labels, 'free' gifts, exaggerated advertisements, fake sales; (8) problems related to services – gas agencies, banks, builders, railways, post, electricity.

Adulteration tests: milk with water – a drop on a tilted plate leaves no trace, or in a tumbler for 10 minutes no ring/cream; black pepper with papaya seeds – in water pepper settles while papaya seeds float; asafoetida with resin or gum – shaken in water pure hing turns milky; tea with coloured exhausted leaves – colour on blotting paper when sprinkled with water; coriander powder with dung powder – smell on soaking in water; spices with extraneous colour – colour in water; tea or semolina with iron filings – a magnet picks them up. Precautions: read labels, check genuine standard marks, buy sealed packs from reputed shops, buy whole spices and grind at home, test samples and send doubtful ones to PFA laboratories. Defective weights: false-bottomed or dented measures, stones as weights, iron rings or magnets under the pan, missing pointer, tilted balance; for cloth – a table used for measuring, bent rod, stretched fabric.

Consumer education tells the consumer what, how much, how, where, when to buy and how to pay: buy only needed things; non-perishables in bulk, semi-perishables for a week, perishables in small amounts; survey the market and read labels; buy from licensed or co-operative shops and from those who replace faulty goods; buy when shops are less crowded; seasonal fruits and vegetables; electronics and woollens off-season; check interest on credit. Consumer aids: labels, leaflets, packages, advertisements, standardisation marks, legislation and consumer organisations. Label information: name, trade and brand name, manufacturer's name and address, ingredients, purpose, directions, warnings, date of manufacture and expiry, dosage, guarantee period, standard mark, MRP, net weight and lot or batch number (needed for complaints; check ingredients for allergies, rates and net amount, expiry).

Standard marks: ISI (electrical goods, chemicals, toys, pressure cookers, biscuits, coffee), FPO (tinned and preserved foods, juices, jams, sauces, pickles), Agmark (spices, cereals, flour, pulses, eggs, oil, butter – agricultural and livestock products), Woolmark (wool and woollen garments), Hallmark (gold ornaments), Eco-mark (environment-friendly goods); ISO 9000 is a global quality-system standard. Packages protect from damage, spoilage, breakage, adulteration and pilferage and help transport. Legislation: the Consumer Protection Act 1986 (amended 2002) covers all goods and services; consumer courts at district, state and national levels. Consumer organisations give information, work for consumer welfare, guide the government, educate consumers, protest against anti-consumer activities, test products and represent complaints in consumer courts.

Rights: safety (against harmful goods such as adulterated food or unsafe appliances); choose (variety of good products); be informed (quality, purity, potency, ingredients, price; e.g. warnings on toxic products, a shopkeeper refusing a pamphlet violates this right); represent; be heard (express in court); seek redressal (against unfair or restrictive trade practices; compensation); consumer education; basic needs (food, clothing, health care, drinking water, sanitation, shelter, education); healthy environment. 15 March is World Consumer Rights Day. Responsibilities: survey the market, insist on and keep the bill, buy standard products, read and follow instructions, buy sealed foods, avoid wastage and hoarding, join other consumers against sellers and file complaints in the proper forum.

Filing a complaint: anyone can file within 2 years of purchase; district forum for goods or services up to Rs 20 lakh, state forum for more than Rs 20 lakh and up to Rs 1 crore, national forum for more than Rs 1 crore; nominal fees; first contact the seller and keep a record, then write to the manufacturer by registered post, then send a notice giving 15 days; fill the prescribed form with facts, attach bills, state the compensation desired and a notarised affidavit; the court notice asks the opposite party to reply within 30 days; cases are to be settled within 90 days (5 months if testing is needed). Relief: removal of defects, replacement, refund, compensation and costs.
